items.title: “Still French, Still Home”: Colonial Citizenship, Family Memory, and Intergenerational Belonging in Franco-India, 1721–1954
items.abstract: Mahé (Mayyazhi), a French enclave on India’s Malabar coast, remained under French administration from 1721 to 1954, and its French-Indian families have carried the legal and cultural consequences of that rule across generations ever since. This study examines how colonial-era intimacy was configured within the broader structures of colonial governance in a small, decentralised enclave largely absent from mainstream accounts of empire. Combining a structured literary analysis of M. Mukundan’s novel On the Banks of the Mayyazhi with ethnographic fieldwork among Mahé’s French-Indian families, the study applies a four-phase Historiographic Narrative Analysis Framework (HNAF) to trace how face-to-face contact, bilingual schooling, and household ritual mediated colonial authority and shaped patterns of loyalty, mimicry, and inherited identity across generations. Fiction and lived testimony reveal overlapping but non-identical traces of an affectively saturated, person-to-person contact zone whose effects outlasted formal decolonisation by decades and continue to shape Franco-Indian family memory and commemorative practice today. The findings suggest that genealogical continuity, rather than political rupture alone, offers a productive lens for understanding how colonial subjecthood is inherited, reworked, and lived within families long after an empire’s formal end. These findings carry implications for the study of other small, materially thin colonial enclaves and for broader methodological debates about using literary sources genealogically. The study also speaks to SDG 10, particularly its emphasis on social, economic, and political inclusion and on reducing inequalities rooted in origin and status, by showing how colonial hierarchies can persist through citizenship, family memory, and inherited forms of belonging.
items.authors: Sayant Vijay

items.title: Bearing Names of the Dead: Memory, Identity Formation, and Family History in Bekwarra Naming Culture
items.abstract: Earlier studies on Bekwarra names have focused on cultural and syntactic perspectives, with limited attention to how the Bekwarra naming culture transmits family history and serves as a cultural archive in which the experiences, struggles, and social roles of departed relatives are encoded. This study, therefore, takes a different direction by showing how name bearers become living extensions of ancestral memory, thereby strengthening and reinforcing kinship ties within the community. Ethnopragmatic theory was adopted as an analytical framework to uncover the cultural meanings embedded in these names. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and informal conversations with 25 participants in Nyanya and Abuochiche Wards, Bekwarra Local Government Area, Cross River State, southeastern Nigeria. The findings reveal that Bekwarra people use naming practices to retain memory, sustain lineage consciousness, and maintain intergenerational connections. Beyond functioning as linguistic labels, Bekwarra names constitute an active social process through which the past informs present identities. To conclude, this study deepens the understanding of the intricate relationship between names, memory, and the ways in which naming acts as a repository of cultural knowledge.
items.authors: Benjamin Okon Nyong, Prince Agbor Onyi

items.title: Comparing LLM and Human Expert Coding in Qualitative Research: A Case Study on Emotional Intelligence
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for qualitative coding, but their ability to recover human-defined construct boundaries remains unclear. Existing studies rarely distinguish thematic granularity from dimension-level semantic alignment. We compare a 12-dimension emotional-intelligence (EI) framework developed from 34 Chinese behavioral-event interviews with three zero-shot LLM analyses of the same corpus under an identical prompt. A structured framework-level mapping procedure classified each human dimension as directly recovered, partially or merged, or not recovered. Alignment was summarized using direct, broad, and frequency-weighted coverage, theme-count precision, and pairwise Jaccard similarities for the three mapping types. Two senior experts evaluated 36 dimension-level relationships, and retained LLM quotations were manually checked against the original transcripts; no fabricated quotations were identified. Direct coverage ranged from 75.0% to 91.7%, broad coverage from 83.3% to 100.0%, and frequency-weighted mapping from 80.3% to 94.9%. Theme-count precision was 50.0% for DeepSeek, 69.2% for Qwen, and 55.6% for GPT. Eight dimensions were directly recovered across all outputs, whereas guidance and motivation, big-picture awareness, care and support orientation, and teamwork varied across outputs. An independent expert reproduced all 36 mappings, yielding 100% raw agreement. The findings distinguish thematic granularity from construct-boundary recovery and support LLMs as complementary analytical assistants.
items.authors: Yuhan Xie, Shifeng Lei, Guang Yang, Feng Yao

items.title: Spiritual Well-Being, Treatment Adherence, and Self-Management in Hemodialysis Care: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hemodialysis requires sustained patient participation in demanding treatment and self-management routines. Spiritual well-being may be a patient-centered psychosocial resource relevant to adherence and self-management, but its independent associations with these patient-reported outcomes remain uncertain. This study examined the associations of spiritual well-being with treatment adherence and self-management among adults undergoing hemodialysis. Methods: This single-center cross-sectional study included 72 adults receiving maintenance hemodialysis at a public hospital in Türkiye between March and May 2025. Spiritual well-being, treatment adherence, and self-management were assessed using the Spiritual Well-Being Scale, End-Stage Renal Disease Adherence Questionnaire, and Chronic Disease Self-Management Scale, respectively. Pearson correlations and two multivariable linear regression models with HC3 robust standard errors were used. Models were adjusted for age, sex, dialysis duration, and number of comorbidities. Rank-based, influence-restricted, and nonlinear sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: Spiritual well-being was positively correlated with treatment adherence (r = 0.822, p 0.001) and self-management (r = 0.891, p 0.001). In adjusted linear models, higher spiritual well-being was associated with greater treatment adherence (B = 4.338, 95% CI 3.550–5.126; p 0.001; adjusted R2 = 0.655) and better self-management (B = 0.494, 95% CI 0.418–0.569; p 0.001; adjusted R2 = 0.787). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the direction and statistical significance of both associations, while nonlinear models suggested attenuation at higher spiritual well-being scores. Conclusions: Spiritual well-being was associated with two patient-reported outcomes relevant to long-term hemodialysis care after adjustment for the measured demographic and clinical covariates. Person-centered nephrology assessment may consider spiritual well-being alongside health literacy, psychological distress, social support, and practical treatment barriers. Longitudinal multicenter studies should determine the temporal direction and clinical implications of these relationships.

items.title: Gout in North America
items.abstract: Gout is the most prevalent inflammatory arthritis in North America, affecting approximately 3.8% of the population in Canada and 5.1% in the United States (US). Epidemiological modeling through 2050 projects that high-income North America will sustain the highest age-standardized prevalence of gout globally. This rising burden is accompanied by heavy socioeconomic costs and striking demographic shifts. Driven by obesity, early-onset gout among American youth escalated by 63% over the last three decades, while nearly one-third of US adolescents now exhibit hyperuricemia, in contrast to ~20% of adults. Furthermore, profound racial inequities persist; Black patients experience a five-fold higher rate of emergency department (ED) visits for gout flares compared to White patients, and older Asian Americans face the highest overall prevalence. Primary care providers manage 70% to 80% of gout cases in both nations. Suboptimal longitudinal care has led to severe reliance on acute services. Post-ED care continuity remains poor, frequently resulting in low rates of follow-up serum urate testing, high readmission rates, and inappropriate opioid prescribing. Diagnostically, polarizing light microscopy of synovial fluid remains the gold standard, supplemented by advanced ultrasound and dual-energy computed tomography imaging, although this technology is limited by provider availability. Treatment paradigms prioritize a treat-to-target strategy to maintain serum urate levels below 6 mg/dL. Allopurinol is the preferred first-line therapy, with recent clinical data validating its safety and efficacy when progressively titrated in patients with chronic kidney disease. Second-line febuxostat requires shared decision making in the context of cardiovascular disease, while advanced, refractory tophaceous gout is managed in the US with intravenous pegloticase which can be co-administered with methotrexate to mitigate immunogenicity. Ultimately, optimizing North American gout outcomes requires improvement in health services delivery with multidisciplinary models of care serving as an emerging solution.
